title: Feasibility of Augmented Reality–Based Motor-Cognitive Training in Parkinson’s Disease, Mild Cognitive Impairment, and Mild Dementia
summary:
People with neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s disease or dementia often experience difficulties with movement, memory, or attention in everyday life. Standard therapies are sometimes not sufficiently related to everyday activities or not motivating enough. As a result, many patients find it difficult to train regularly and make progress.
We are therefore testing a new training approach using augmented reality. Augmented reality means that digital content and exercises are projected into the real environment using special glasses. This is intended to train movement and thinking at the same time in a way that is as close as possible to everyday life.
The study is aimed at inpatients with Parkinson’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, or mild dementia. Recruitment and participation take place during the inpatient stay at RWTH Aachen University Hospital. Before the training begins, short assessments of memory, attention, and movement are carried out. Participants then complete up to five training sessions using augmented reality glasses. During the training, they interact with virtual objects and playful exercises designed to support movement, attention, and reaction skills at the same time. In addition, questionnaires are used to assess how patients experience the training.
In this study, we investigate whether this type of training can be used well in clinical practice and is well accepted by patients.

interventions.name: Patients with diagnosed neurocognitive and neurodegenerative conditions (i.e., Parkinson’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, or mild dementia) will receive an augmented reality–based motor and cognitive training program (up to five 30-minute sessions over two to three weeks).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Patients with a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease (Hoehn and Yahr stages I–IV) or patients with a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild dementia.
2. Patients must be able to understand the purpose and risks of the study and provide informed consent.
3. Sufficient proficiency in German to communicate effectively and to complete the questionnaires and assessments used in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Balance disorders
2. Confounding neurological conditions (e.g., history of traumatic brain injury), neglect, or moderate to severe dementia or cognitive impairment that would interfere with study participation
3. Blindness or severe visual impairment
4. High risk of falls or motor impairments in type or severity that could interfere with the successful completion of the training
5. Psychiatric or behavioral disorders that may interfere with the study procedures, or acute suicidality
6. Known seizure disorder (epilepsy)
7. Other significant medical conditions that, by their nature or severity, could interfere with the study or influence the outcome measures
8. Presence of implants or medical devices that preclude the use of an AR headset
9. Persons involuntarily detained by judicial or official order
